messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Product Manager
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ezequiel was only 22 when the shelling of his neighborhood hit the apartment building that housed him and his parents. The blast was not the first—there had been weeks of artillery fire, of sirens wailing from a distance—but that night the sound of a mortar shell, a low, guttural boom that rattled the windows, jolted him awake. He remembered the flash, the brief, incandescent curtain of light that painted the ceiling in an unnatural orange, and the shockwave that made his chest feel as if it were being crushed. In the days that followed, the memory of that night lingered, a sharp, unfiltered echo that would come unbidden whenever a sudden clatter or the hiss of a car engine in the street sounded too close. Ezequiel’s body remained on alert. The muscle tone in his shoulders did not slack even while he sat at his desk at the tech firm where he worked as a product manager. He walked into meetings and felt the urge to scan the room, noting every small movement—a colleague shifting in a chair, a child’s laugh from the break room, the faint creak of the office door. In one meeting, when a co‑worker asked a question, Ezequiel’s gaze darted to the corner of the room where a projector screen glowed. The sudden shift in light startled him so much that he reached for the razor in his drawer, cut a small line on his wrist, and felt the sting release a wave of panic that, oddly, made him feel a momentary sense of control. The self‑harm was his way of interrupting the relentless, unmediated fear that he could not escape. He often told the therapist that “the cutting helps because it’s a different kind of pain—one he can see and touch.” That same self‑harm routine would become a habit he followed whenever the startle reflex was triggered, whether it was the sound of a car engine or the sight of a passing bicycle. The repeated pattern reinforced a belief that his body would never be safe, that any unexpected movement could be a threat. This belief was the core of his hypervigilance: his mind was constantly scanning for the next potential danger. The cycle tightened when the visible scars and bandages began to appear on his forearms. When he saw a new bandage or felt the rough edge of a bandage's adhesive, Ezequiel’s body automatically tightened again, his heart racing as if an invisible enemy was approaching. The presence of the scar reminded him of the potential for sudden harm, even when there was no immediate threat. He began to think, “If I am not watching, something will hit me.” That thought fed into his threat perception, raising the threshold for what he considered dangerous. The more he cut, the more he felt the need to be on guard. He found himself looking over his shoulder as he passed through the office lobby, the sense that someone might be watching him as a hidden threat. The anxiety about being potentially harmed intensified his body monitoring, causing him to check his heart rate and look for bruises before, during, and after every task. The fear that his body might betray him made it harder for him to concentrate on the product roadmap presentations he was supposed to lead. He avoided front‑row seating at meetings, preferring the back where he could see the room from a distance, his body always tense, always ready to react. By the time he scheduled his first therapy session, Ezequiel’s symptoms had escalated. He had missed two important sprint reviews because the prospect of speaking in front of his team triggered an overwhelming startle response that left him shaking and unable to articulate his ideas. The therapist noted that his self‑harm had become a nightly ritual—an attempt to release a pressure that he could not otherwise manage. He also reported frequent reassurance‑seeking, constantly asking teammates if he was doing “the right thing” or if his body had “reacted in the wrong way.” Those moments of seeking external validation were not isolated; they were attempts to confirm that his perception of danger was warranted. Yet the reassurance only reassured him of his vulnerability, further entrenching the threat mindset. The cycle had become so entrenched that the moment he stepped outside the office to grab a coffee, he would find himself staring at the street, listening for the slightest movement, his body trembling as if an explosion could erupt at any second. When he had to attend a client presentation, he would check his pulse, feel the bandage on his arm, and feel the dread that his body might fail him. The most painful moment for Ezequiel was the realization that he could not simply "shake it off." He had become a product manager in the literal sense of managing his own product—the product of his own fear—yet he could no longer see the way forward without the constant presence of a threat. He reached out for help because he feared that the cycle would swallow him entirely, that he would lose the ability to contribute to his team or to live outside of the panic that now governed his days. He hopes, though, that with therapy he can break the loop, learn to trust his body again, and reclaim the product roadmap that he once envisioned with enthusiasm.
